アナ と もうします — My name is Ana

You speak modestly about what you do (謙譲語): まいる, おる, いたす, もうす, いただく, はいけん する, うかがう, ぞんじる and the form お～する / ご～する; you learn the “us and them” rule (うち と そと): when talking to an outsider, you speak humbly about your boss and your family.
to receive; to eat, to drink (humble)
to let someone know, to contact
to hold back, to politely decline
Pleased to meet you. I’m Ana, his wife.
I came to Bucharest in September this year.
If anything comes up, I’ll let you know right away.
Ionescu said he’d be a little late.
To understand what 謙譲語 does: you lower yourself (and your group) to raise the other person.
To use the special humble verbs: おる, まいる, いたす, もうす, いただく, はいけん する, うかがう, ぞんじる, さしあげる, おめに かかる.
To form the regular humble form: お + stem + する / いたす (おまち します) and ご + noun + する (ごれんらく します).
To apply the うち と そと rule: when talking to an outsider about your boss or your family, you use humble forms and drop “-san”.
To stop mixing up 尊敬語 and 謙譲語 (✗ はいけん して ください) and to give a polite self-introduction.

Wednesday evening, at a small Japanese restaurant in Bucharest’s old town. Mr Tanaka has invited Mihai, Ana and Dr Ionescu. He’s already waiting for them in a private room. Mihai and Ana arrive first; Ionescu comes a little later. As last time, Dr Ionescu’s lines (in Romanian) are written in plain Japanese.
Mr Tanaka, I’m sorry to have kept you waiting.
Not at all, I’ve only just arrived myself. …And this must be your wife?
Pleased to meet you. I’m Ana, his wife. I’m from Spain.
I’m Tanaka. How are you feeling? Please don’t overdo it today.
Thank you. I’m well, thanks. I’m so glad you invited us today.
I’m terribly sorry. Ionescu said he’d be a little late.
That’s no problem. Come, please help yourselves, don’t be shy.
Would you like some sake, madam?
I’m sorry, I’ll pass for now. Could I have some tea?
(Coming in, in Romanian) Sorry I’m late. Mihai, introduce yourself: tell him you’re the one in charge of the new device.
Mr Tanaka, allow me to introduce myself once more. My name is Mihai. Until August I worked at a hospital in Madrid.
I will be in charge of the new device. I look forward to working with you.
Likewise. Well then, here are the materials on the new device.
(wrong) Thank you. Then, Mr Tanaka, please “humbly look” at them too.
(Laughing) Mihai, “haiken suru” is the word for when YOU look.
Oh no, I’ve done it again. …Then I’ll look over them.
Not at all, you speak much better than the day before yesterday. If there’s anything about the device, please contact me any time.
Thank you. If I have any problem, I’ll let you know right away.
Mr Tanaka, may I ask what your granddaughter’s name is?
Yes. My granddaughter is called Hinata. “Hinata”, as in a spot where the sun shines.
What a lovely name. I’d love to meet her one day.
“omatase itashimashita” = sorry to have kept you waiting
Ionescu (without “-san”: Mihai’s boss, talking to an outsider)
“enryo naku” = without holding back; “enryo itasu” = to hold back
“yoroshiku onegai itashimasu” = I look forward to working with you
moh-shi-mas: a long “mō”, worth two syllables; a short “shi”. Don’t say “mo-shi-mas”: without the length it sounds like “moshi moshi”.
i-ta-shi-mas, i-ta-da-ki-mas: they start the same, so listen to the third syllable: “shi” = I do (いたす), “da” = I receive (いただく).
ha-i-ke-n: “ha-i” are two separate syllables, not a short “hi” as in English. wa-ta-ku-shi: the “ku” is almost whispered, wa-tak(u)-shi.
1. 謙譲語: you lower yourself to raise the other person

In chapter 36 you raised the other person (めしあがる, いらっしゃる). Now you do the opposite: you step down a level yourself. 謙譲語 (けんじょうご) is used for YOUR actions (or your group’s), especially when they concern the respected person: you tell them something, visit them, receive something from them, show them something.
the guest, the boss, the client

English has a few traces of polite humility too: “allow me to introduce myself”, “may I humbly suggest”, “your humble servant”, and even “ciao” comes from “(I am your) slave”! Japanese kept it in the verbs: the same “I say” becomes もうします when you speak to someone important.
You’ve been using 謙譲語 for ages without knowing it: いただきます before a meal literally means “I (humbly) receive”. And もうします (my name is) has been around since chapter 14.
2. The special humble verbs (and their respectful partners)

As with 尊敬語, the most common verbs have special words. They’re easiest to learn in pairs: the ordinary verb in the middle, the respectful one on the left (for the other person), the humble one on the right (for you).
きく / たずねる (to visit)
いただく has two humble meanings: “to receive” (= もらう) and “to eat / to drink” (= たべる / のむ). And うかがう has two as well: “to ask / to hear” and “to visit”: あした うかがいます = I’ll come to see you tomorrow.

おる and まいる are also used as “neutral” politeness, not just humble, in announcements: でんしゃ が まいります (the train is arriving), ゆき が ふって おります (it’s snowing). That’s why you hear them so often at stations and on the phone.
3. The regular form: お + stem + する / いたす
For other verbs: お + stem (～ます without ます) + する. With いたす instead of する it becomes even more polite. With Sino-Japanese する verbs you use ご: ごれんらく する, ごあんない する, ごせつめい する.
I’ll let you know the result.
I’ll show you around the hospital.

The phrase from the start of the dialogue comes from here too: またせる (to make someone wait, the causative of まつ, ch. 33) → おまたせ いたしました = “I (humbly) made you wait”, i.e. “sorry to have kept you waiting”.

お～する is only used when your action is DONE FOR or DIRECTED AT the other person. “Let me carry your luggage” → おもち します ✓. But “I walk” doesn’t concern anyone: ✗ おあるき します. And it doesn’t work with one-syllable stems (みる, いる, ねる): for those there are はいけん する, おる.
4. うち と そと: “us” and “them”

This is the most unusual part for an English speaker. In Japanese, the world is divided into うち (your group: family, colleagues, company, even your boss) and そと (outsiders: clients, guests, other companies). When you speak to someone from そと, your whole group “steps down” with you: even your boss.
outside: the boss is “one of us”, no せんせい / さん, humble form

The same goes for family: to an outsider you say はは (my mother), ちち (my father), つま (my wife), まご (my granddaughter) and use humble forms. About the OTHER person’s family: おかあさん, おくさま, おまごさん and respectful forms. That’s why Mr Tanaka says まご は ひなた と もうします, while Ana says おまごさん の おなまえ.
I’m Ana, his wife. (Ana about herself)
Dr Ionescu isn’t at the hospital right now. (on the phone, to an outsider)

In English it would sound rude to call your boss just “Ionescu” in front of a client. In Japanese it’s the other way round: if you say イオネスクせんせい が おっしゃいました in front of a client, it sounds as if you’re putting your boss above the client. Every language has its own logic.
5. Pitfalls: don’t mix the two up
The most common mistake foreigners make (Mihai included!) is using humble forms for the other person or respectful forms for themselves. Always check: WHO is doing the action?
イオネスクせんせい が いらっしゃいます。 (to a client)
For “I” in very formal situations, use わたくし. Apologies also go up in steps: すみません → もうしわけ ありません → もうしわけ ございません.

Don’t overdo it! One humble or respectful verb per sentence is usually enough. Too much keigo (おまち いたさせて いただきます…) sounds stiff or even sarcastic. Among friends and family, keigo creates distance: Ana only speaks keigo to Mihai as a joke.

こころ の ある けいご — Keigo with heart
On Tuesday at six in the morning, Mihai and Ana were sitting in front of the computer. In Tokyo it was one in the afternoon.
On the screen, Yuki laughed as she ate her obentō. “A keigo lesson? Leave it to me.”
Ana, drinking a warm milk, opened a new notebook.
When she first joined the publisher, apparently, the editor-in-chief often told her: “Your keigo is a mess.”
“The most important thing is ‘us and them’. When you talk to someone from outside, even your boss is ‘one of us’.”
“So in front of Mr Tanaka, even about Mr Ionescu you say: ‘Ionescu (humbly) says…’.”
Mihai put his head in his hands. “Call my boss by his bare name? In Romania I’d be fired on the spot.”
Yuki laughed and went on: “Then, about yourself you speak from below. ‘Ikimasu’ becomes ‘mairimasu’, ‘iimasu’ becomes ‘mōshimasu’.”
“What should I say?” Ana asked. “‘Tsuma no Ana to mōshimasu’ is enough.”
“Now the editor-in-chief even praises me sometimes.” As she said that, someone called her from behind. “Oh, my lunch break is ending! Good luck!”
Ana wrote “mōshimasu”, “mairimasu”, “itashimasu” in big letters in her notebook and read them aloud many times.
“Spanish has ‘usted’ too, but for all the words to change… Still, it’s fun.”
On Wednesday evening, the two of them went to a small Japanese restaurant in the old town.
Mr Tanaka was already waiting for them in the back room.
When they came in, Mr Tanaka stood up and bowed politely. Ana wanted to bow deeply too and, because of her big belly, wobbled a little.
“Oh, please, there’s no need! Sit down, please.” Mr Tanaka hurriedly brought her a floor cushion.
As soon as he looked at the menu, Mr Tanaka called the waiter right away. “The lady mustn’t have raw fish. Tempura and udon, please.”
Mr Tanaka had thought of it before Mihai, who was the doctor. Ana’s heart warmed at such kindness.
A little later, Dr Ionescu came in, looking cold.
The doctor said, in the Japanese he had just learnt from Mihai, “Good evening. Sorry to have… kept you waiting”, and bowed awkwardly.
Mr Tanaka was very pleased and bowed back even more deeply.
During the meal, Dr Ionescu talked at length, in English, about his dreams for the new device.
At the hard parts, Mihai helped in Japanese: “Ionescu (humbly) says he wants to train young doctors with this device.”
After saying it, Mihai gave a start. He had called his boss by his bare name and, on top of that, used “mōshite orimasu”. Exactly as in Yuki’s lesson.
Dr Ionescu, who had no idea, heard his name and nodded happily. Ana hid her mouth behind her napkin and held back her laughter.
After the meal, Mr Tanaka showed them a photo of his granddaughter on his phone.
It was a lively-looking little girl with a school satchel on her back. In her hand she held a keigo card just like Mihai’s.
In the corner of the card a small sunflower had been drawn.
Ana smiled and said: “I’ll send Hinata a postcard from Spain. One with a field of sunflowers.”
“My granddaughter will be delighted. Thank you.” Mr Tanaka bowed his head, visibly pleased.
“By the way, have you already decided on a name for the baby?” “No, we’re still thinking about it together.”
“Once she’s born, please do show me a photo.” “Yes, we’ll definitely send you one.”
When the bill came, Mihai quickly took out his wallet. “Mr Tanaka, today we…”
But Mr Tanaka waved his hand. “Today I’m the one who invited you.”
Mihai put his wallet away and bowed deeply. “Then, thank you for treating us.”
Outside, a cold wind was blowing. Before getting into the taxi, Mr Tanaka shook Mihai’s hand.
“Mihai, your keigo still has mistakes. But it has heart. That’s what matters most.”
The three of them stood in the street until the taxi was out of sight. Dr Ionescu, still a little awkward, kept his head bowed too.
Then the doctor said to Mihai, in Romanian: “I didn’t understand a word of your Japanese. But one look at the director’s face was enough. Well done.”
On the way home, Ana held on to Mihai’s arm and said, as they walked:
“Today I said ‘mōshimasu’ five times.” “And I got ‘haiken’ wrong once.”
They both laughed. Mihai looked at Ana’s belly and said: “I wonder if she’ll struggle with keigo one day too.”
“Don’t worry. We’ll teach her. Making mistakes ourselves now and then.”
In the square, preparations for the Christmas market had already begun and lots of little lights were twinkling.
The next evening, a photo of a letter arrived by email from Mrs Fumiko, who had already come to Madrid to stay with her sister.
In beautiful handwriting, it said: “At the beginning of December, my sister and I are coming to Bucharest. It will be our first trip together as sisters.”
“I would like to offer your neighbours some tea from Kyoto too. We are leaving Tama in Kenji’s care.”
At the end of the letter, in Mrs Suzuki’s slightly shaky handwriting, there were just a few words: “I am so looking forward to it.”
Ana and Mihai looked at each other. “Looks like our keigo practice isn’t over yet.”
